name: Bulldozers, Bullets, and the Constitution
description: About the LectureFor the last decade or more, the Indian Constitution has played a starring role in the romance of the Indian nation, especially among those who identify as liberals. This lecture sounds a more pessimistic note. It focuses on Article 21, the article that purports to protect life and personal liberty — and asks what its well-documented inadequacies actually mean.A clear view of these gaps should make us question the idea that the Constitution is a solution to our contemporary troubles. In some respects, it may be part of the problem.The session explores:Why Article 21's protections of life and personal liberty are, in practice, woefully inadequateWhat the gap between constitutional promise and constitutional practice revealsWhy treating the Constitution as sacred might get in the way of confronting its limitsHow "colonial law" and the history of civil liberties shaped the Indian constitutional traditionAbout the SpeakerArudra Burra has a background in political philosophy and law. He wandered into Indian constitutional history while working on questions involving the idea of "colonial law" and the history of civil liberties in the Indian constitutional tradition — concerns he is currently exploring in a book project titled Constitutionalism before the Constitution. He is also interested in the connections between Western and Indian philosophical traditions, explored most recently in his paper "What is 'Indian' about Indian Political Thought?" He teaches in the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences at IIT Delhi.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony
description: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Thursday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.3rd September: Dr. Rahul KapoorWomen, Work and Well BeingWomen's participation in paid and unpaid work shapes far more than a household budget, it shapes physical, psychological, economic, and social well-being all at once. But that participation is rarely on equal terms: wage gaps, occupational segregation, invisible care work, and the daily balancing act between job and family all take a toll. Dr. Rahul Kapoor, Assistant Professor of Sociology and Social Work at Gautam Buddha University and author of Women and Work: The Sky is Full of Sexism, asks what a genuinely gender-sensitive approach to employment and social protection would actually look like — and why economic participation alone was never going to be enough.17th September: Anukriti AgarwalChacha Knows Best: Chacha Chaudhary and the Politics of NostalgiaBefore Indian households had cable or the internet, they had Chacha Chaudhary — a turbaned uncle whose brain worked faster than a computer, created by Pran Kumar Sharma in 1971. Fifty years on, that same deliberately ordinary uncle now sells toilets, water conservation, and voter turnout on behalf of government ministries. Anukriti Agarwal, a language educator and Fulbright Fellow at Yale, traces how a comic-book uncle went from newsprint to nation-building — and what it reveals when a state borrows the nostalgia the middle class grew up on.24th September: Dr Shashank SinghPrinces in the Polls: Indian Royals and Inherited Power in a Democratic Age, 1948–1967Between the 1950s and 60s, former princely elites didn't disappear from Indian politics — they reinvented themselves within it. Dr Shashank Singh, Junior Fellow at the Prime Ministers Museum and Library and a historian of Gwalior's princely order, uses electoral data and legislative debate from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh to show how monarchical charisma and patronage fused with electoral legitimacy. His argument: India's democratic consolidation didn't dismantle the feudal order so much as absorb and repurpose it.

name: UNSENT: A 2040 Safety Hackathon
description: What if, in 2040, nobody had to say, “Text me when you get home”?UNSENT is a speculative safety experience that asks participants to imagine a future where the conditions that make this sentence necessary have disappeared. Rather than designing better ways to check in, participants work backwards from this imagined 2040 to uncover what had to change in our streets, public spaces, mobility systems, technology, policies, social norms and cultures of care.Through lived experiences, speculative scenarios, collective mapping and system-building, participants explore where safety currently breaks down, how people compensate for it, and who or what they depend on to feel safe. They then build competing visions of 2040, testing each against questions of freedom, risk, access and control.The ideas generated are captured in the 2040 Safety Atlas: a collective map of safety gaps, dependencies, interventions, stakeholders and trade-offs.At its heart, UNSENT asks a simple but provocative question:What would have to change today to build a world where nobody needs to text when they get home?

name: In the Language of Home: A Poetry Workshop
description: Dillipoetry, in collaboration with Exhibit 320, presents In the Language of Home — a poetry workshop designed as an immersion into the ongoing exhibition Mool, curated by Shaleen Wadhwana. The workshop invites us to create a space where poetry becomes a portal into our own stories of origin and belonging, with visual art and the company of kindred voices guiding us along the way.The ​poetic experience ​resides within the expansive group exhibition, bringing together 20 artistic voices from across South Asia. Together, these works explore how lived experiences of cross-border yearnings, shared geographies, language, and community shape the ways we mourn, love, play, dress, build, eat, move, dream, celebrate, and hope.As Shaleen Wadhwana, curator of Mool, writes: “South Asia is not an easy term to define because there is a painful gap between those who carelessly drew its cartographic boundaries without ever visiting the region and those who carry its meaning and live its reality.” ​While also noting that the region always had its own documented and lived histories of language, art, culture, history, and heritage.Over two hours, ​the workshop will take us through reflective prompts and guided writing exercises promising to hold up a slow melding of personal, intergenerational, and maybe collective.​As we immerse ourselves in the visual worlds of artists across borders, we will sing, play with and respond to some ​of the wisest voices like Amrita Pritam, Faiz, Agha Shahid Ali, Kamala Das among others​, showing us a glimpse of their home.About the host: Rachit is a poet and the founder of Dillipoetry, a literary platform known for its thematic and experimental poetry walks, workshops, and training programmes. He previously served as Creative Head at Youth Alliance, where he designed and facilitated leadership journeys for young social leaders across India. With over a decade of experience in the social development sector, his work engages a range of social concerns, and his poetry has appeared in over 25 literary platforms and anthologies. His recent series Memories of Yami and The Asthma City, tracing the Yamuna River and Delhi’s air crisis, were published in Down To Earth magazine.He has been selected for international residencies, including Language is a Queer Thing by The Queer Muslim Project in collaboration with the British Council, UK, and is a recipient of the Germinator Grant by Ecoversity for Dillipoetry’s regenerative arts practice. Rachit has performed at BBC Contains Strong Language (Leeds 2023, Bradford 2025) and at institutions such as the French Institute India, Goethe-Institut, British Council, and Alliance Française, with his work also featured on BBC Radio 3’s The Verb. He has served as Lead Poet and Advisor to O.P. Jindal Global University’s programme We Are Meant to Sing as One.About Exhibit 320: Exhibit320 is a contemporary art gallery based in New Delhi’s Lado Sarai district. Over 16 years, the gallery has developed a dynamic program of solo and group exhibitions, long-term artist collaborations, and discursive events, engaging both established and emerging South Asian artists. The gallery continues to foster critical inquiry, experimentation and intergenerational dialogue, expanding the possibilities of contemporary visual culture locally and globally.

name: When AI Starts Inventing
description: When AI Starts Inventing: How AI Is Cracking Problems That Have Resisted Us for Decades, and How to Bring It from Big Tech's Labs to Your LaptopIn September 2026, OpenAI announced that a team of AI agents had produced a proof, machine-verified in Lean, for a problem about how fluids move that has stood open for ninety years and carries a million-dollar prize. Before that, an AI agent found a faster way to multiply matrices, the operation that sits underneath almost all modern computing, beating a record set in 1969. It is starting to feel routine: every few weeks, another problem that resisted people for decades quietly falls to an AI agent.How does this actually happen? That is what we will look at first, because the mechanism turns out to be stranger and simpler than most people expect.Then a harder question. Every time the agent is asked to produce something, someone pays, and the more capable the AI, the higher the bill. A single discovery run makes thousands of such calls, which is why almost all of this work happens inside a handful of enormously wealthy labs. In our lab we are trying to change that, and doing so means asking questions nobody bothers to ask when the budget is unlimited. Does every step really need the most expensive AI model, or would a cheaper one do just as well? Is every attempt the agent makes actually worth making? Our investigation of these discovery pipelines, across several notoriously hard problems, reveals that around 98% of the AI agent's calls contribute nothing to the eventual solution. And they still succeed. Which leaves a genuinely open question: is that waste the price of discovery, or simply a bill nobody has bothered to reduce?About the SpeakerProf. Sayan Ranu is the DS Chair Professor in AI at IIT Delhi, jointly appointed in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering and the Yardi School of AI. His research focuses on machine learning for structured data, particularly graphs, and increasingly on AI systems that can reason, plan and discover solutions on their own. His work spans automated algorithm discovery, AI agents, self-supervised learning and trustworthy AI. His research has been published at leading AI and machine learning conferences including NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR and KDD. Looking at them afresh means asking the questions they've spent centuries deflecting: the role of women, the contribution of the dispossessed, and the quintessential human questions of survival and existence.A feminist retelling brings the women back to the centre. It strips away the proverbial sheen of the "just" war to focus on the human question underneath. Whether it's the fiery Draupadi, the "manipulative" Satyavati, the warrior queen Chitrangada, Janaki, or the duo of Kaikeyi and Manthara, the Epics allow us to deconstruct these women through a modern feminist lens.The session explores:How feminist retellings of the Mahabharata and Ramayana recentre their women charactersWhat writers like Tagore, Mahasweta Devi, Irawati Karve and Chitra Divakaruni reveal through their retellingsWhy the Epics' "timeless" characters remain contemporary and urgently relevantHow deconstructing canonical narratives changes what the stories are actually aboutAbout the SpeakerDr. Nandini C. Sen is a Professor of English at the University of Delhi — an author, editor, literary critic and storyteller. For nearly three decades, she has explored how literature shapes the way we understand history, identity, gender and the world around us, working across African Literature, Diaspora studies, mythology, postcolonial studies and feminist readings of the Indian epics. Her academic journey has taken her from Delhi to London as a Charles Wallace Scholar, to the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla as a Fellow, and to universities and literary forums across the world. She is the recipient of the Write India Award for creative writing, the Ambassador for Peace Prize for teaching in a slum cluster, and the Best Lecturer's Award from the Government of Delhi. She is the author of the bestselling short story collection The Second Wife and Other Stories, and editor of several acclaimed books.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. description: Nani ka Ghar by V's Supper Stories A supper brunch of home-cooked nostalgia.Some recipes don't survive migration. They get left behind in old kitchens, remembered only in fragments- a smell, a story, a dish someone's grandmother used to make that no one quite knows how to recreate anymore.Nani ka Ghar is a supper built around dishes like that. Rooted in Multan, where my own Nani is from, and reaching into Lahore and Sindh - the homes our grandparents carried with them. This menu brings back food that's slow, laborious, and increasingly rare: a sourdough flatbread fermented over three days, a lotus-stem starter barely made anymore even in Sindhi households, a moth dal kachori you'll mostly only find on a handful of old Delhi streets.Alongside them sit the dishes that never left, a rich Lahori chicken karahi, a comforting channay, and phirni made exactly the way it's made every Holi in our family, because some things don't need reviving. description: Sentirenla Lucia is a vocalist, vocal coach and performing artist specializing in R&B, Neo-soul and Contemporary Jazz. She works with singers focusing on healthy vocal technique, musicality, confidence and individual expression. She continues to perform whenever the opportunity arises. Many students that she has mentored have been accepted into prestigious Music Colleges such as Berklee College of Music, Oberlin Conservatory of Music, BIMM etc. with scholarship under her tutelage.Lucia began performing and recording professionally in New Delhi, working on jingles and television projects that received nationwide radio and television airplay. In 2002, she became a founding member of Artistes Unlimited, a 60-member choir and charitable trust, collaborating with artists including Shubha Mudgal, Parikrama and composer Julius Packiam. She has also performed with Them Clones and other leading musicians.In 2005, Lucia received a scholarship through Berklee College of Music’s World Scholarship Tour. She graduated from Berklee in 2010 with a degree in Vocal Performance. During her time there, she performed at the Berklee Performance Center, sang background vocals for artists including Tata Vega, Rhiannon and Larry Watson, and shared stages with Lalah Hathaway, Amel Larrieux, Esperanza Spalding and Eguie Castrillo. She also worked as a session vocalist and was selected to sing in a tribute to Angelique Kidjo at Berklee’s graduation ceremony.Lucia has taught and performed in both India and the United States. In Boston, she taught private voice and directed a cappella ensembles at Zumix, City Music – Berklee College of Music and School of Groove. She has also performed with Jazz Urbane, Semper Soul, The Singing Tribe and Sung Deep, and founded Phoenix Anthology to promote musical diversity and create opportunities for musicians from Nagaland. After she received her Artist Visa she taught private voice lessons and background. She also had the privilege to attend a workshop with Bobby McFerrin, who is her inspiration and since then has been on the journey to discover every aspect of vocal training attainable.Lucia hopes to inspire and motivate those who may have lost their sense of purpose through music, while continuing to learn, perform and contribute to a more diverse and expressive musical community.

name: Body Language Speaks Louder Than Words
description: About the LectureA raised eyebrow. A shift in posture. A half-second pause before an answer. Long before you finish a sentence, your body has usually already told the room the truth.This lecture explores body language as one of the most powerful forms of communication we have. From micro-expressions and eye movements to posture, gestures and the subtle inconsistencies between what someone says and what they do, we'll examine how non-verbal cues reveal emotion, confidence, stress and intention long before words catch up.Drawing on years of training law enforcement, forensic and academic institutions across India — from the Delhi Police Crime Branch to CISF and the CBI's forensic science laboratory — and on his recent analysis of world leaders at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Gaurav Gill takes the same tools used in interrogation rooms and diplomatic summits and turns them toward everyday life: negotiations, dates, interviews, and the conversations you have every day without realising how much you're saying.The session explores:How facial expressions, posture and gestures reveal what words often hideThe difference between a nervous habit and a genuine sign of deceptionHow law enforcement and forensic experts read non-verbal cues in real investigationsPractical ways to apply body language reading to your own personal and professional lifeAbout the SpeakerGaurav Gill is a body language expert and consultant psychologist who has trained several of India's most prestigious law enforcement, forensic and academic institutions. In September 2026, WION News invited him to analyse the non-verbal communication of global leaders at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, decoding the handshakes, gestures, posture, facial expressions, eye contact and physical proximity behind high-level diplomatic engagements. He has also featured on Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast, in an episode that has drawn more than 2.9 million views.His training assignments include the Delhi Police Crime Branch AHTU, Delhi Police (Central District — Kamla Market, Hauz Khas and IP Estate), Pune Police and Pune Crime Branch AHTU, SPUWAC Headquarters (Special Police Unit for Women and Children), the Railway Protection Force (RPF), Government Railway Police (GRP), CISF and the CISF ASG Unit. He has conducted specialised body language training for forensic experts at DFSS-CFSL (formerly CBI-CFSL), New Delhi, and has been guest faculty at the National Forensic Sciences University (Delhi and Goa campuses), Rashtriya Raksha University (Gujarat campus) and the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB-VII), Dwarka, Delhi.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Cultures Through Clay: Civilisation Held In A Bowl
description: About the LectureWe sometimes just think of pots as functional. But across three cultures — Bangladesh, Turkey and Japan — the same simple act of shaping wet clay reveals three completely different value systems: community and belonging, beauty and craftsmanship, imperfection and impermanence.This talk isn't really about pottery. It's about how to read the objects around us, and what your own everyday things might be quietly saying about you.Drawing on folklorist Henry Glassie's The Potter's Art, the session zooms into three pottery traditions: in Bangladesh, pottery woven into caste, community and everyday ritual life; in Turkey, pottery as a vessel for aesthetic pride and decorative mastery; and in Japan's Hagi tradition, tied to the tea ceremony, where the values invert entirely — imperfection, asymmetry and impermanence, the wabi-sabi aesthetic, are not flaws to correct but the entire point.The session explores:How the same craft, shaping wet clay, produces radically different worlds of meaning across culturesWhat pottery in Bangladesh, Turkey and Japan reveals about caste, beauty and impermanenceWhy folk art is never really anonymous, static or purely functionalWhat your own everyday objects might be quietly saying about what you valueAbout the Speaker Simran Sushila is a folklorist and a professor, currently pursuing her PhD in Folklore at Indiana University Bloomington, USA. Her research looks at how communities use tradition to make sense of identity, memory, belonging, and change....and then, somewhere along the way, the she became an entrepreneur. Years of teaching and evaluating students made her increasingly curious about something: how does a person take what they know – and make another person see it, understand it, and believe it?That question became The VoiceCraft Institute: her attempt to build something India doesn't quite have yet – a serious space for learning expression, language, and communication, beyond grammar classes and beyond test-prep English.Because knowing English is one thing. Knowing what to say, how to say it, and how to make it land – that's a craft. name: Designing Your Life, The Stanford Way
description: About the LectureWhat if the life you're living right now is one you drifted into by default, not one you chose?We are born into stories, about success, work, money, relationships, identity and what a good life should look like. Somewhere along the way, those stories start to feel like our own, and a life shaped by default begins to feel like one shaped by choice.Stanford's Designing Your Life offers another way to look at it: life as something you can actively design. That doesn't mean finding one "true" self or one perfect path. It means moving towards self-authorship: questioning the narratives you inherited, imagining different futures, and accepting that there may be more than one life within you worth living.Design turns out to be an unusually useful lens for this, because it doesn't require you to know the answer before you begin. It lets you work with ambiguity, hold several possibilities at once, and experiment rather than predict. In a world where lives are increasingly nonlinear, that may be more useful than having a perfect plan.The session explores:How inherited social narratives quietly become the stories we live byWhy there may be more than one life within us worth livingHow designers work with ambiguity, and why that matters for life decisionsMoving from a life by default to a life by design: question, imagine, prototypeAbout the SpeakerNavyug Mohnot is a Stanford-certified Designing Your Life educator, coach and facilitator, a visiting faculty member at ISB and Ashoka University, and the founder and CEO of QAI Global. name: Can We Make Delhi a Human City?
description: Welcome to Human City Conversations where we have intimate conversations about how cities are built, how they are lived, and who gets to shape them.Conversation 1: HOW DO WE MAKE DELHI A HUMAN CITY?Delhi is a city of contradictions. It has some of India's best public institutions, an expanding metro network, enormous infrastructure projects and a new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 that sets out a vision for how the city should grow and change over the next two decades. And yet, the experience of living in Delhi can be very different.Millions of people spend hours commuting across the city. Walking can feel like an afterthought. Public spaces are often unevenly distributed and poorly connected. For many women, moving through the city comes with a calculation of safety that men may never have to make. And then there is the air. Every winter, Delhi's air pollution becomes a public health crisis forcing a city of millions to think about something as fundamental as whether it is safe to breathe outside.So how can a city with so much planning, infrastructure and investment still struggle with some of the most basic conditions of everyday urban life? Perhaps the problem is not simply how much we build, perhaps we need to ask a more fundamental question:What kind of city are we actually trying to build? And more importantly, who is that city being built for?For the first Human City Conversation, urbanist Jagan Shah joins Ruchita Bansal for an open conversation about Delhi, its future and the gap between the city we plan on paper and the city people actually experience. We'll explore what makes a city genuinely liveable from mobility and housing to public space, safety, air pollution and neighbourhoods and look at what Delhi's new Master Plan for 2047 could mean on the ground.What to ExpectA curated, open conversation between urbanist Jagan Shah and Ruchita BansalA look at Delhi's urban future and what the new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 could mean on the groundA discussion about the gap between the city we plan and the city people actually experienceA closer look at how cities are shaped by policies, infrastructure and development decisionsPerspectives on what makes a city genuinely liveable, accessible and inclusiveA 30 minute Q&A SessionInformal discussion and one on one conversation after the conversationEvent Details📅 Sunday, 11 October 2026🕔 5:00 PM onwards📍 Kunzum Books, GK II, Delhi☕ Your ticket includes one coffee/tea .About the SpeakerJagan Shah is an urbanist, architect and former Director of the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), with decades of experience working at the intersection of urban planning, policy, governance and development. He has been closely involved in shaping India's urban policy and planning landscape, including work connected to Delhi's Master Plan, the Smart Cities Mission and other national urban development programmes. His work has involved developing and implementing policies and frameworks that influence how Indian cities grow, transform and respond to the challenges of rapid urbanisation.Over the years, Jagan has worked across urban planning, housing, infrastructure, heritage, governance and institutional development, working with governments and institutions at different levels.His experience spans both the making of plans and policies and the realities of implementing them, making him particularly well placed to examine the gap between the city we envision on paper and the city that people actually experience.About the ModeratorRuchita Bansal is an architect and urban planner with 15 years of experience working on cities, urban development and planning policy. Her work has ranged from developing planning frameworks and regulations to working directly on large-scale urban transformation projects. She was part of the team behind Ayodhya Vision 2047, working on one of India's most complex and rapidly transforming urban environments and seeing first-hand the challenges of translating ambitious plans and visions into reality on the ground.Today, Ruchita is the Creator and Host of The Human City Podcast and the founder of SheCity India, using conversations, research and storytelling to make urban planning more accessible and bring the discussion about cities beyond the professional planning community. Through The Human City, she explores a simple but often overlooked question: what does all this planning mean for the people who actually live in our cities?Note: Attendance implies consent to being filmed for event documentation. If you do not wish to be filmed, please reach out to your curator for the evening, Ruchita. Come curious. Come questioning. Come ready to talk about the city we call home.

Despite his young age, he has participated in and won several state-level music competitions and is also a Sangam Kala Group winner.His soulful and soothing voice has earned him appreciation and blessings from renowned personalities of the ghazal and music fraternity, including Ustaad Ghulam Ali Khan Sahib and Murshid Ali. His musical journey is deeply rooted in the guidance of his guru, Sh. Sudhanshu Ehsaas, who has been nurturing and training him since Yashraj was just six years old.The talent that Yashraj displays today is the result of years of dedicated riyaaz, discipline, learning and hard work—both by the young artist and his guru. His understanding of music, command over ghazal and Sufi compositions, and his naturally peaceful and expressive voice make him a truly promising young performer. Depot 48 provide talented singers and performers with a platform where they can build their artistic profile, gain confidence and, most importantly, experience the energy and dynamics of a live audience.For Yashraj, this opportunity is especially meaningful. At just 12, he already possesses the musical ability of a seasoned young artist, while live audience engagement is naturally an area where he will continue to grow with experience. With more stage exposure, interactions with diverse audiences and continued riyaaz, he has immense potential to develop into a confident and compelling live performer.
